title: String Quartet in F major
hook: Written at 28, dedicated to Fauré, and modelled on Debussy, yet unmistakably Ravel’s own.

painting.title: The Evening Air
painting.pairingNote: A calm, classical scene of figures under pines at dusk, built from small separate touches of pure colour; like Ravel’s quartet, an old, orderly form seen in new light.

facts: Ravel wrote the quartet in Paris between December 1902 and April 1903, when he was 28. It is dedicated “to my dear teacher Gabriel Fauré”, his composition teacher at the Paris Conservatoire.

It was first played on 5 March 1904 in Paris by the Heymann Quartet, at a concert of the Société nationale de musique. Fauré was not much taken with it. Debussy was: on the eve of the premiere he wrote to Ravel urging him to change nothing.

The plan follows Debussy’s String Quartet of ten years earlier: four movements, a plucked [[scherzo|scherzo]] in second place, themes that return across the work. But the sound is Ravel’s own: clearer, cooler, and more tightly built.
Critics were divided. One said it bore “an incredible resemblance” to Debussy; another called Ravel “one of the masters of tomorrow”. It has remained a standard work of the chamber music repertoire.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a gentle song in sonata form (I), a plucked dance with a slow, wistful heart (II), a dreamy night piece (III), a storm in five beats that calls back the opening (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato – Très doux
movements.summary: Ravel marks the opening *très doux*, “very sweet”, and the whole movement keeps that soft, glowing tone. It is a classical [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with two themes. The surprise comes near the end, when the second theme returns transformed by a change in just one of the four parts.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1
mainIdeas.description: a long, calm tune in the first violin that rises and falls in one smooth arc, while the other three move quietly in step beneath it.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a sadder, more inward melody, played by the first violin and the viola together, two octaves apart.

stops.hear: All four play softly; the first violin sings a long tune that climbs and falls back, the others gliding underneath
The tune moves on while the second violin and viola ripple in quick, light notes
A sudden surge, faster and louder, to a short burst at full strength
Calm again: the first violin and the viola sing a sadder melody together, high and low
Fragments of both themes drift through new keys; the four lines grow more tangled
The loudest passage of the movement, with fast, insistent chords, then a long easing off
The opening tune returns, soft and unhurried, as at the start
The sad melody comes back, but now warm and in F major
stops.happening: Theme 2 changed: the upper three parts are as before; only the cello has moved, a few notes higher

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: Slower and quieter; the movement fades on a soft chord

notice: Compare Theme 2 at ≈ 1:45 and ≈ 6:50. The violin and viola play the same notes both times; only the cello changes, and the colour turns from shadow to light.
Listen for how rarely anyone plays loudly. Ravel keeps the volume low for most of the movement, so the few outbursts stand out.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Quartetto Italiano recorded the quartet in Switzerland in August 1965, coupled on the original LP with Debussy’s quartet. On the Spotify album the quartet is tracks 1–4, followed by Ravel’s Violin Sonata (Arthur Grumiaux) and Piano Trio (Beaux Arts Trio).

movements.heading: Assez vif – Très rythmé
movements.summary: A [[scherzo|scherzo]] that opens with all four players plucking their strings. The rhythm is the game: the music is written in 6/8 and 3/4 at the same time, so the beat seems to shift every few bars. In the middle the dance stops for a long, slow, muted song led by the viola.

mainIdeas.name: The plucked dance
mainIdeas.description: a quick, dry tune in A minor, all [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]. Some writers hear in it the Javanese gamelan, which Ravel heard in Paris in 1889; others hear Spain.

mainIdeas.name: The bowed melody
mainIdeas.description: a smooth, singing line that floats above the plucking.

mainIdeas.name: The slow song
mainIdeas.description: a wistful tune, first in the viola, with the instruments [[muted|muted]].

stops.hear: All four players pluck a quick, dancing tune; the accents keep slipping between two and three beats
stops.happening: The main theme, in [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]. The two metres pull against each other, a [[hemiola|hemiola]]

stops.hear: The first violin picks up the bow and sings a long, smooth line over the plucking
The plucked dance again, growing louder, with bowed and plucked notes mixed
Everything slows; with mutes on, the viola sings a slow, sad tune
The song passes between the instruments over soft, rippling figures; it pushes forward, then holds back
The quick plucked dance returns

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A rush to a loud, sharp ending

notice: Tap your foot to the opening. Every few bars the music seems to swap a beat of three for a beat of two, without ever losing its pulse.

movements.heading: Très lent
movements.summary: A slow, dreamy movement with the instruments [[muted|muted]]. It is restless rather than calm: Ravel changes the tempo again and again, and the music keeps drifting away from its key. It is linked by its themes to the first movement.

mainIdeas.name: The viola’s song
mainIdeas.description: a long, sorrowful line over soft chords.

mainIdeas.name: The rocking figure
mainIdeas.description: quick, quiet repeated notes played over the fingerboard, under a rising melody.

stops.hear: Muted and very slow: soft chords in the violins and cello, and the viola sings a long, sorrowful line
stops.happening: The first theme, introduced by the viola

stops.hear: A soft plucked chord and a pause, then a quick rush of notes that falls back
stops.happening: One of many sudden changes of tempo

stops.hear: The first violin takes over the viola’s song
Mutes off: louder and more urgent, with firm chords
Mutes on again; a soft, rocking pattern of quick notes, and above it a melody that swells
The fullest, most passionate moment of the movement
Quiet again; the opening song returns
stops.happening: The return of the opening (*1er Tempo*)

stops.label: Last 45 seconds
stops.hear: Very slow, muted chords fading away

notice: Listen to the chords in the opening minute. Ravel moves them in parallel, which the rules of harmony forbid, and they sound open and old, almost like a chant.

movements.heading: Vif et agité
movements.summary: A finale like a squall: tremolos, sudden accents and an uneven five-beat rhythm. It is loosely a [[rondo|rondo]], with calmer episodes between the outbursts. In one quiet passage the gentle first theme of the first movement floats back, tying the whole work together.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: fast, sawing repeated notes ([[tremolo|tremolo]]) in groups of five, loud and urgent.

mainIdeas.name: The long melody
mainIdeas.description: a broad, singing line that rises above the agitation.

mainIdeas.name: The memory
mainIdeas.description: the first movement’s opening tune, very soft.

stops.hear: Loud, sawing repeated notes in all four instruments, in a lopsided five-beat rhythm
The storm drops; a long, singing melody rises over a rippling accompaniment
stops.happening: The calmer second idea, now in a slower 5/4

stops.hear: Very quiet, played over the fingerboard: the gentle tune from the very start of the quartet
stops.happening: The first movement’s Theme 1 recalled, an example of [[cyclic-form|cyclic form]]

stops.hear: The storm breaks out again
All four players hammer out the melody at full strength
A brief hush, very soft
stops.happening: The last calm before the end

stops.label: Last 15 seconds
stops.hear: A final rush and loud chords in F major

notice: Count the beats in the opening: five to a bar, grouped unevenly. It is what makes the storm feel off balance.
When the first movement’s tune returns, notice how far away it sounds, played softly over the fingerboard.

threads.title: Four equal voices
threads.body: No player simply accompanies for long. The viola leads the slow song in the scherzo and opens the slow movement; the cello’s single change transforms the first movement’s second theme.

threads.title: The opening tune
threads.body: The first movement’s Theme 1 echoes in the slow movement and returns, far away, in the finale.

threads.title: Clarity
threads.body: Ravel takes Debussy’s plan but writes with sharper outlines: clear phrases, classical forms and precise sounds, plucked, muted or played over the fingerboard.
